A1. Empowerment describes a person's ability to have choice and control of the activities in their life. **

Empowering actions

  • providing information so that a person can make an informed choice
  • giving praise and celebrating successes
  • getting to know the person and considering their individual needs and preferences
  • offering choices
  • providing opportunities for learning and developing new skills.

Disempowering actions

  • telling people what option is best for them
  • being critical
  • making choices for the person
  • not treating someone as an individual
  • completing tasks without asking permission
  • completing tasks that the person does not require assistance with.

A2. History of the disability sector And the Aged Care Sector

Listen: History of the disability sector (about 2 minutes)

Listen: History of the Aged care sector (about 2 minutes)

Recent developments – disability sector

As of July 2023, there are around 4.3 million Australians who have a disability. The National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) will provide approximately 460,000 Australians aged under 65, who have permanent and significant disability, with funding for supports and services. For many people, it will be the first time they receive the disability support they need.

Recent developments – Aged care sector

Over the years residential aged care and home and community organisations have been established to provide 24/7 support to older Australians.

Home and community organizations expanded in both size and number. Previously volunteer-driven, these organizations now employed staff, offering career pathways and a wider range of services.

2015: Introduction of CHSP

In July 2015, significant changes reshaped the aged care community sector, now known as the Commonwealth Home Support Programme (CHSP). These changes included updates to accreditation standards, funding models, and reporting practices for residential services.

2018: Royal Commission Launch

In 2018, a Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety began. The final report, delayed until 2021 due to COVID-19-related challenges, addressed issues like infections and deaths in residential aged care services.

2023: Aged Care Reforms

The aged care reforms started in 2023. These included a new funding and reporting model, adjustments to staffing ratios and pay rates, the implementation of SIRS (explained in this unit), and the creation of an Aged Care Code of Conduct. More changes are expected to enhance service quality for both users and staff in the coming years.

Models to describe disability

Shifting Disability Lenses

A3. These models show how people used to think disabilities were punishments from God or illnesses. Now, we understand that it's more about how society treats and includes people with disabilities. The newer models focus on empowering individuals, celebrating diversity, and ensuring equal human rights for everyone, regardless of disability.

Religious Model:

  • This is an old idea that says if someone has a disability, it's a punishment from God for the person or their parents' past mistakes.
  • Some people believed that having a disabled child is a special blessing from God.
  • This way of thinking made people with disabilities seem different and not equal in the community.

Medical Model:

  • This model became popular as medical knowledge increased.
  • It sees disability as an illness that needs to be taken care of.
  • People with disabilities were labeled based on the type of disability they had.

Social Model:

  • This is a more modern way of thinking.
  • It says that the disability itself is not the main problem; it's the barriers and attitudes in society that create the difficulties.
  • Discrimination, exclusion, and limitations come from society, not just the person's condition.
  • The goal is to empower people with disabilities and include them fully in society.

Identity Model:

  • Building on the social model, this one emphasizes that society creates barriers for people with disabilities.
  • It encourages a positive view of disability, seeing it as a valuable part of human diversity.
  • People with disabilities have unique experiences, strengths, and contributions to society.

Human Rights Model:

  • Combines elements from the social and identity models.
  • Emphasizes that everyone, regardless of disability, has the same human rights.
  • Disability should not limit a person's rights.

**

**Human rights are like the building blocks of a supportive relationship. They mean that a person's rights are always thought about and protected in every step of getting help. This includes picking the right service, developing an individualised plan, choosing what kind of help they want, and how they want it. Human rights influence how staff and the person getting support, talk and work together.

**

Social justice has made a big impact on how we treat older people and those with disabilities. It has led to: **

  • Advocacy: People now have someone to speak up for them. This person, called an advocate, helps them understand and express their needs and rights. Advocacy ensures everyone has control over their own lives.
  • Empowerment: This means giving people the strength and ability to make their own choices. Empowered individuals feel confident and capable. Social justice focuses on making sure everyone has the tools and support to reach their goals and live the way they want.

These changes also:

  • Address inequalities in how resources and support are given.
  • Make services more flexible and centered around each person's unique needs.
  • Fight against ageism and ableism, making sure older people and those with disabilities are valued in communities. This opens up job opportunities and ensures equal treatment when accessing services or being part of the community. **

Models of Support

A4. Institutionalised Care: **

  • This is an old way of providing care from the early 20th century.
  • It is a medical model for disability - taking care of a group of people in a structured and organized place
  • The focus is on quickly meeting their needs, often using strict rules.

Person-Centred Approach: **

  • This is about planning and making decisions together with the person needing support.
  • The person sets their goals and preferences, approves strategies, and can change their mind.

Strengths-Based Approach:

  • Everyone has strengths that can be used for well-being.
  • It's about identifying and building upon these strengths, making tasks more successful.

Self-Directed Model of Support: **

  • The person manages their own support decisions, including staff, funding, and therapies.
  • It can be fully self-directed or involve some help from family or a plan manager.

Active Support:

  • Key Idea: Remember the motto "do with, not for."
  • Explanation: Instead of doing everything for someone, support workers help with tasks the person can't do. This support builds a foundation for the person to learn and develop skills.
  • Challenge: It's important not to focus only on completing tasks quickly or being overly helpful. The goal is to let the person play an active role in their own life.
  • Benefit: When a person is actively involved, their self-worth increases compared to being a passive participant.

Normalisation:

  • In the 1960s Bengt Nirje developed the concept of normalisation. It began in times of widespread institutionalisation of people with a disability. At this time, people's lives were overly regimented, excessively structured and did not reflect real life. The idea was to make life more normal for people in care.
  • This means regular routines, diverse experiences, and exposure to everyday living.

Social Role Valorization (SRV):

  • Many people with disability had their shopping done for them, barely showed their face in the supermarket, would have someone else attend to their needs and would only occasionally attend public events, indicating that a person with disability did not have a valued role in the community. Follow the Normalisation the social role valorisation (SRV) was developed by Wolf Wolfensberger in the 1970s, SRV values and supports people with disabilities in meaningful social roles.
  • It fights against societal devaluation and promotes inclusivity.

Active listening requires more than just hearing. It requires the listener to focus on the words that are being said, how they are being said, the person's facial expression and body language. Once the speaker has finished, the listener will need to objectively analyse each portion of the message. Did the words and the way they were spoken match the person's body language and facial expressions? What is the person really saying?

A4.2 Examples of action or task which demonstrates a support worker using that model of care

Rights-Based Approach:

  • Reminding people they have rights, helping them contact an advocate if needed, and assisting in making complaints if their rights are not respected.
  • Ensuring the person knows they can participate in decisions, experience non-discriminatory service, feel empowered, and have services that are accountable.

Strengths-Based Approach:

  • Working together with the person and those supporting them to determine outcomes based on the person's strengths.
  • Identifying and using the person's strengths and assets to achieve positive results.

Person-Centred Approach:

  • Listening, thinking together, coaching, sharing ideas, and seeking feedback. Taking time to focus on the person and personalizing interactions.
  • Ensuring decisions about the person's life involve them at the center, treating them as an individual rather than a task to be completed.

Human-Rights Based Approach:

  • Empowering people to know and claim their rights in all aspects of life and support services.
  • Ensuring that individuals are aware of their rights and supporting them in exercising those rights.

Self-Advocacy:

  • Representing oneself or expressing one's views and interests.
  • Encouraging and supporting individuals to speak up for themselves.

Active Support:

  • Empowering people with disabilities to do things for themselves instead of staff doing it for them.
  • Creating opportunities for individuals to actively participate and engage in tasks, promoting independence.

Active Listening:

  • Fully concentrating on what is being said, using all senses to understand the speaker's message.
  • Actively engaging in listening rather than just hearing, demonstrating genuine interest in the person's communication.

Definitions

Access to services, resources and opportunities that aid in a quality, meaningful life.

Equality as in people all having the same rights and circumstances.

Equity as in fairness.

Access and equity do not refer to all people being treated equally when accessing services. It relates to treating people fairly to ensure that they have the equal ability to access the services they require. Access and equity eliminate the barriers present when people are trying to access services, by levelling the playing field.

Empowerment

A5. Empowering Actions and Practices: **

Being Heard: People feel empowered when they are listened to, and their decisions are respected.

Knowing About Advocacy: Having information about advocacy empowers individuals to speak up for themselves.

Tailored Services: Services are more empowering when they are personalized to meet individual needs.

Active Participation: Empowerment involves allowing active involvement through real conversations.

Assessing Abilities: Understanding what a person can do with the right support is part of empowerment.

Informed Choices: Providing information helps people make choices based on understanding.

Praise and Celebrations: Acknowledging successes through praise fosters a sense of empowerment.

Knowing the Person: Empowerment comes from getting to know the person and considering their unique needs.

Disempowering Actions and Practices:

Deciding for Others: Telling people what's best for them takes away their control.

Being Critical: Being overly critical diminishes confidence and empowerment.

Making Choices for Them: Choosing without involving the person disempowers them.

Not Seeing Them as Individuals: Treating someone as if they're the same as everyone else takes away their uniqueness.

Task Completion Without Permission: Doing tasks without asking first takes away the person's choice.

Unnecessary Assistance: Helping with tasks they can do themselves is disempowering.

Limiting Choices: Not offering options or asking permission restricts independence.

Talking Down: Speaking in a condescending way reduces a person's sense of empowerment.

Talking About, Not With: Discussing a person in their presence makes them feel excluded.

Using Baby Talk: Treating adults like children can be demeaning.

Ignoring Rights: Not informing or upholding rights undermines empowerment.

Disregarding Choices: Ignoring or not respecting the person's choices diminishes their autonomy.

Advocacy

A6.

  • Definition: Advocacy is speaking up for someone to protect their rights and interests.
  • How It's Done: After talking with the person and getting permission, an advocate becomes their voice.
  • When It's Needed: Advocates help those who may be vulnerable, disempowered, or unable to speak up on their own.
  • Beyond Individuals: Advocates also work to change society's views through public education and campaigns for policy and law improvements.

Types of Advocacy:

  • Self-Advocacy: This is when a person speaks up for themselves, asserting their rights, expressing needs, and making decisions about their life.
  • Family Advocacy: In this situation, a family member is given authority to represent and support the person in asserting their rights and making decisions.
  • Individual Advocacy: A professional advocate provides support, information, or skill-building to help a person receiving individual support become more capable of self-advocacy.
  • Citizen Advocacy: Similar to individual advocacy but usually involves a volunteer without formal training. They support a person in identifying situations of abuse or denial of human rights and help protect their well-being.
  • Legal Advocacy: Provided by a professional advocate specializing in legal matters. They can represent a person in court, helping them communicate effectively and explain situations to facilitate positive changes for a group of disadvantaged people.
